entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: The first trained character LoRA works, verified by looking
entries.body:
VIRO trained: 1000 steps, rank 16, 16 images, 9.8 minutes at 1.74 it/s, 97.7 MB.

A bug that made it look like nothing happened: SaveLoRA writes relative to ComfyUI OUTPUT,
not models/. So a successfully trained LoRA landed in output/loras/ where LoraLoader
cannot see it, and the tool reported no LoRA appeared. train_character.py now moves it
into models/loras and confirms ComfyUI can see it.

VERIFIED BY PIXELS, not a loss curve. Same prompt, same seed, IPAdapter forced to zero so
the LoRA is the only thing acting on identity, in a scene deliberately NOT from the
training set - a rainy neon street.

  without   a generic dark-haired figure in a black coat, anonymous, far from camera
  with viro the two-tone curly hair, the teal top with orange collar, his face

Both failure modes are excluded. It is not undertrained: the pair differs completely. It
is not overfit: the scene and pose are new rather than the training portrait returning.
That distinction is the whole reason the test scene is unfamiliar - a familiar one would
have hidden memorisation, which with only 16 images was the likely failure.

Honest drift: the garment reads as a green long-sleeve rather than a numbered soccer
jersey. That is faithful to the turnaround set it learned from, not a training fault -
the turnaround itself had drifted the costume, which is the thing to fix upstream.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Use a trained character LoRA in the actual film render
entries.body:
This is what the cast pipeline was for. compile.py now emits character_loras for any
cast member that has one, and short.py inserts it between the checkpoint and the sampler
on every beat that character appears in.

Until now identity in a film rested entirely on IPAdapter refining a face from one
reference sheet - and a weight sweep on this box found the character was ALREADY
RECOGNISABLE AT ZERO, meaning the sheet was carrying far less than assumed and faces
drifted between shots regardless. A sheet is a hint. A trained LoRA is a change to the
weights, and it holds in scenes the sheet never covered.

Both run together: they refine the same thing from different directions and the sheet
costs nothing once a LoRA is present. Strength defaults to 0.85, overridable per film
via character_lora_weight - a character LoRA is a taste dial, unlike an accelerator LoRA
which has exactly one correct value.

The LoRA node is inserted by rewiring whatever consumed the checkpoint MODEL output,
rather than by assuming node order, so it stays valid if the base graph changes.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Add lora_check: prove the character LoRA with pixels, not a loss curve
entries.body:
A loss number cannot tell you whether a character LoRA is good. Its two failure modes
are both invisible in a metric and both obvious in a picture:

  OVERFIT       it reproduces the training images. Ask for the character somewhere new
                and you get the training portrait back, pose and crop and all.
  UNDERTRAINED  it changes nothing; the with/without pair is the same picture.

lora_check renders the SAME prompt at the SAME seed with and without the LoRA and tiles
them. IPAdapter is forced to weight 0 so the LoRA is the only thing acting on identity -
otherwise the reference sheet would mask exactly what is being tested.

The test scene is deliberately NOT one from the training set. A familiar setting hides
memorisation, which is the failure most likely here with only 16 images; an unfamiliar
one exposes it in a single glance.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: A cast page, and the first LoRA this project has ever trained
entries.body:
/cast shows the people in your films as reusable identities rather than descriptions you
retype. Each card carries what actually exists for that character - identity tags, the
damage ladder, a voice, a reference sheet, the turnaround views, and a trained LoRA once
there is one - and says plainly which of those are missing.

The views are DISCOVERED from samples/cast/<id>/ rather than recorded on the card, so the
page cannot claim a turnaround that was deleted. Same reason the LoRA is only reported
after training has written it onto the card.

Opening a character shows the three stages of making them consistent, each with the
command that runs it, and each honest about what it buys:

  1 reference sheet   one portrait. IPAdapter refines a face from it - but a weight sweep
                      on this box found the character "already recognisable at ZERO", so
                      a single sheet carries less than you would think.
  2 turnaround        16 views, framing held constant. A far stronger reference, and the
                      training set.
  3 trained LoRA      the character stops being a prompt and becomes a model.

TRAINING IS REAL. Verified running, not just submitted: 231/1000 steps at 1.74 it/s,
loss moving between 0.04 and 0.40, GPU at 79% and 322W, 20 GB VRAM, about 10 minutes for
1000 steps on 16 images. This is the first use of ComfyUI's native training nodes in this
project - the LoRA-training capability folder has said "not-explored" since it was
written.

MANAGER is the useful counter-example on the page: no reference sheet, so IPAdapter
drops to weight 0 on every shot of him and his face drifts. The card says so rather than
looking complete.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Turnaround and character LoRA training - the two pieces the cast idea needs
entries.body:
TURNAROUND. workflows/32_qwen_turnaround.json chains
qwen-image-edit-2511-multiple-angles-lora after the 4-step accelerator, so one picture of
a person becomes many views of THAT SAME PERSON rather than new people who match the
description. The LoRA has been on disk unused since it was downloaded.

studio/_tools/turnaround.py drives 16 authored views - angles, then expressions - and
writes a caption per image. Verified on VIRO: identity holds across front, three-quarter,
both profiles, back and looking-up. Same two-tone curly hair, same face, same jersey.

A bug worth recording, because it is the same one this project keeps making. The first
run left framing to the model: "side view ... full profile" was read as FULL BODY, so
those two views zoomed out and lost the costume entirely while the head-and-shoulders
views held perfectly. Two things varied and only one was intended. Framing is now written
into every prompt, and the two deliberate framing changes are named and kept to a
minority of the set - because a LoRA learns whatever the set holds CONSTANT as the
character and whatever it varies as not the character.

TRAINING. workflows/33_train_character_lora.json is the first thing in this project to
use ComfyUI's native training nodes, which have been installed and unused the whole time:

    LoadImageTextDataSetFromFolder -> MakeTrainingDataset -> TrainLoraNode -> SaveLoRA

Defaults are deliberately NOT the node's. steps 16 is a smoke test that produces a LoRA
changing nothing; 1000 for a 16-40 image set. rank 16 rather than 8, because a face needs
more capacity than a style. learning_rate left at the node default, since it is the
parameter most likely to need tuning against real output and inventing a better one
without measuring would be the exact mistake recorded elsewhere in this repo.

The dataset is staged into ComfyUI/input, because the loader offers a dropdown of
directories there and a set anywhere else is invisible however well formed. Verified:
viro_train now appears, 16 complete pairs.

Why this matters: every consistency mechanism here so far works around not having it.
Tags describe a person and do not make the same face twice, and a weight sweep on this
box found the character "already recognisable at ZERO" IPAdapter - the single sheet was
carrying far less than assumed. A character that is a prompt cannot reliably be the same
person; a character that is a trained model can.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Make verify legible and reversible
entries.body:
Two things were wrong with asking someone to judge these.

FIRST, no stated failure modes. "Why might these be wrong?" is the right question and
the page did not answer it. It now lists the five that have actually happened here:
a none option that shows the effect anyway because SDXL cannot negate (77 panels);
two options that are the same instruction written twice; an option that contradicts the
fixed subject and gets resolved at random; everything moving because any clause change
re-rolls the whole image; and options written in camera jargon the model does not read.

The point being: this is not grading art. It is spotting mechanical failures, and they
look like "these two are the same picture" or "nothing changed".

SECOND, it implied permanence. A verdict is data - stored with who set it and when,
visible in a git diff, replaced by answering again. The page now says so, shows your
previous answer on any card you return to, and has an "already answered" tab so you can
revisit and change anything. Nothing here is a ruling.

The claim is also now labelled "what this setting is supposed to do", because the
intention was on the page but never named as such.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Rewrite verify so it can be answered without knowing the terms
entries.body:
The first version asked "does extreme_wide work?" - unanswerable unless you already know
what extreme_wide should look like, which is exactly what the cards exist to TEACH.
Requiring the knowledge first was backwards.

The question that matters most needs no expertise at all: ARE THE OPTIONS DIFFERENT FROM
EACH OTHER? A variable whose options render identically is broken whatever the labels
mean, and that is the most common defect in this set - 133 of 134 cards were already
suspected of it. So that is now question one, in plain words:

  "Are these 7 pictures different from each other?
   Ignore whether they look good. Could you tell them apart with the labels removed?"
     Yes clearly / Some are, some look the same / No, all the same / Not sure

Question two is optional and guided: each panel now shows THE CLAUSE IT WAS ASKED FOR
(present on 95% of the 1049 panels), so you can judge a picture against its instruction
without knowing the vocabulary. Click any that look broken or duplicated.

Question three is free text in plain words - "the last two are identical" is a perfect
answer.

"NOT SURE" IS NOW A FIRST-CLASS ANSWER on both queues. It records that a human looked and
could not judge, WITHOUT writing a verdict, and leaves the card in the queue. A wrong
verdict is worse than none here: every predicted verdict in this project that was later
checked against pixels turned out wrong, which is the whole reason human review exists.

Tag examples got the same treatment - the entry's "what it means" and "so the right-hand
picture should look..." are shown above the pair, and the question is just whether you can
see that difference. Its two rejections are now phrased as observations rather than
diagnoses: "they look the same" vs "they differ, but it looks bad".

entries.subject: A verify page, and a base prompt that was rendering below the project's own standard
entries.body:
WHAT I NEEDED WAS EYES, so this makes that cost seconds. /verify walks two queues:

  Capability cards   134 with panels and no human verdict. works / mixed / fails, plus
                     click any option that is broken or indistinguishable from its
                     neighbour, plus a free-text "what to notice". Keyboard 1/2/3/s.
                     The verdict is written into the card's own JSON with verified_by
                     "human" - because every predicted verdict in this project that was
                     later checked against pixels turned out WRONG, and that distinction
                     needs to survive in the data.

  Tag examples       does the pair actually demonstrate the tag? Two DIFFERENT rejections,
                     because they are different problems:
                       "doesn't show the tag" - the comparison failed; the base already
                         had the effect, or composition moved too much to read
                       "looks like slop"      - the comparison worked but the picture is
                         not worth showing
                     Both reroll on a new deterministic seed. The second also increments
                     slop_rerolls on the tag, so one that keeps producing weak images can
                     be found later and given a better base rather than rerolled forever.

THE TAG BASE WAS BAD, and by my own hand. It read "1boy, solo, short dark hair, plain
jacket, standing, city street, daytime" - correctly neutral for isolation and completely
lifeless. Worse, it omitted the four quality tokens that this project measured as
LOAD-BEARING ("without them output is markedly softer and flatter"), so every pair was
rendering below the standard of every other image here.

The tension is real: isolation wants a plain base, a glossary worth looking at wants a
striking one. The resolution is composition, not style - a real subject, a real light
source, a real depth cue, the quality block restored, and still no rendering style, lens
or mood named, because those remain the tag's job. All 89 pairs re-rendering.

Note on "delete the weak ones": weak is a finding about the MODEL, not a defect in the
entry. That `cinematic` does almost nothing is one of the more useful things here - it is
in the house style of every film and has been doing nothing. Deleting those entries would
make the glossary lie by omission. The images are what get deleted and rerolled.

rendering below the standard of every other image here.

striking one. The resolution is composition, not style - a real subject, a real light
source, a real depth cue, the quality block restored, and still no rendering style, lens

entry. That `cinematic` does almost nothing is one of the more useful things here - it is
in the house style of every film and has been doing nothing. Deleting those entries would
make the glossary lie by omission. The images are what get deleted and rerolled.

entries.subject: A glossary: what every tag means, and a picture of what it does
entries.body:
"cel shading" appeared in the house style field of every film with nothing anywhere
saying what it meant or what it did. Same for every other tag in the project.

studio/tags/ is a glossary. Each entry answers three things in order - what the WORD
means, what it DOES to the picture on this model, and when to reach for it - plus how
strong the effect is, what it pairs with, what it fights with, and whether it belongs in
the NEGATIVE prompt instead.

studio/_tools/tag_examples.py renders a with/without pair for every entry: identical base
prompt, identical seed, identical sampler, one clause added. Negative-only tags are paired
the other way round (absent vs present in the negative), because putting them in the
positive is the mistake the entry exists to warn about.

WHY A PAIR AND NOT A GALLERY. "Here is a picture that used cel shading" teaches nothing -
you cannot tell which part came from the tag. Holding everything else still is the only
way the difference is attributable.

AND WHAT THE PAIR DOES NOT PROVE, said on every card rather than left to be discovered:
composition still moves between the two panels, because adding any clause re-rolls SDXL's
conditioning even at a fixed seed. So read the shading, colour and line - not the pose.
An img2img pass from one fixed base would isolate it properly; that is not built yet.
This is the same limitation that makes 133 of 134 capability cards prove nothing, and
claiming otherwise here would repeat it.

/tags is searchable by term, family and strength. Every page now links to every other:
library, direct a scene, make, tags, gallery.

Seeded with cel_shading and motion_blur (the documented negative-only case) to prove the
renderer; the rest of the glossary is being authored now.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Video length is authorable, every page links to every other, and you can read the graph
entries.body:
CLIP LENGTH. clip_secs was hardcoded to 6 for every shot in every film. It is now a
variable at any level plus a per-shot override:

    clip_secs: 4                                    scene / chapter / movie
    shot: sakuga @push @8s | leaping volley, ...    this shot only

@-tokens parse in any order - a camera name or a duration. Above 10s it CLAMPS with a
reason rather than silently mangling: LTX quantises to 8n+1 frames at 24fps and drifts
past about 10s, so a 30s request becomes 10s and says so. Verified: 4s->97 frames,
8s->193, 2s->49, 30s->clamped to 241.

Worth knowing when choosing: LTX cost is nearly FLAT in length - 193 frames measured
13.7s against 97 frames at 13.5s - while an extra shot costs a whole keyframe plus a
whole clip. Asking for more seconds is the cheap way to buy edit room.

NAVIGATION. /make existed for several commits with nothing linking to it. Every page now
reaches every other: library, direct a scene, make, gallery.

WORKFLOW PREVIEW. A "Preview workflow" button on /make shows the exact ComfyUI graph a
generation would submit, without submitting it - the resolved values first, then the
graph - plus a JSON download and a link to ComfyUI. It is built by the SAME code path
that runs it, so it cannot drift from what actually executes; a separate preview
implementation would eventually lie. ComfyUI takes the download directly via
Workflow -> Load (API format).

entries.subject: Four voices in the library did not work at all, and nothing said so
entries.body:
--vary voice generated nothing while sfx and music worked. My own logging hid why: the
script piped through `grep -E "voice__|generated|skipped"`, so the traceback matched
nothing and vanished. That is the same mistake as a monitor that only greps for success -
silence read as "no output" when it meant "it died".

Unfiltered, ComfyUI was rejecting the path: the four vibevoice entries are real files on
disk but are NOT in the accepted list for UnifiedTTSTextNode. Querying /object_info shows
the node takes 21 values; the library listed 25. Picking one of the other four failed
MID-RUN rather than at pick time.

The library is now reconciled against ComfyUI rather than against the filesystem - the
node is the authority on what it will take. Those four are marked `unsupported` with the
reason, and --vary skips three statuses instead of one:

  blocked      a clone of a real person; the craft notes forbid casting it
  unsupported  the file exists but the node rejects it
  roadmap      not implemented

25 voices: 17 castable, 4 blocked, 4 unsupported.

Example cards generated for every castable option, everything else held still:
17 voices, 20 sfx, 8 music cues. All 17 voices generated, 0 failed, 47.8s.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Five makers on one engine: voice, music, sound, stills and 3D
entries.body:
The film wizard needed a timeline and a MOVIE>CHAPTER>SCENE hierarchy. Voice, music,
sound effects, single images and 3D assets do not - they are one artifact with
parameters. Forcing them into the film schema would be the wrong shape, so they get
flat makers that SHARE the libraries, the gallery and the provenance record.

ONE RUNNER, NOT FIVE. These differ in exactly three ways: which ComfyUI workflow runs,
which node inputs the fields map to, and what comes out. All three are now data in
studio/domains/<id>.json, so a sixth domain is a JSON file rather than a feature.

  studio/domains/          five descriptors, node maps READ OUT OF the workflow JSON
  studio/_tools/domain_gen.py   generic runner; --vary steps one library through every
                                value with everything else held still, which is what
                                makes a capability card mean anything
  studio/make.html + /make      one generic page driven by whichever descriptor you pick
  /api/domains, /api/make       answered inline, because these are SECONDS not minutes:
                                3s a voice line, 7.6s a music cue, 4.5s a still

Verified end to end through the API, not just the CLI: music 394 KB, sfx 84 KB, voice 3.0s.

Everything lands in the SAME manifest the film gallery uses, so one page browses films,
stills, voices, cues and meshes together and every artifact carries the settings that
made it.

HONEST LIMITS, stated in the descriptors and shown in the UI before you touch anything:

  mesh   GEOMETRY ONLY. Hunyuan3D 2.1 emits a POSITION attribute and nothing else - no
         UVs, no texture, no vertex colour, no normals, ~525k tris. TripoSplat emits a
         splat with no faces. NEITHER IS GAME-READY; both need retopology and texturing.
         Good for blockouts, silhouette reference and 3D-print bases.
  voice  the 8-dimension emotion vector exists only on indextts2. On higgs_v3 an emotion
         is recorded and does nothing, and the field says so.
  sfx    one sound per generation - the model cannot layer.
  image  past ~2 MP this model duplicates composition; generate at 1-2 MP and upscale.

Four voice packs are clones of real people and are marked blocked - the picker disables
them rather than quietly offering them.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: A film no longer has to be anime
entries.body:
compile.py hardcoded keyframe_engine="anime" at line 471, so every film authored in this
format went through animagine-xl-4.0 whatever it was about. short.py has ALWAYS had the
other branch - 13_qwen_t2i_styled and 14_qwen_edit_ref, driven by Qwen-Image 2512 - and
the authoring layer simply could not reach it. Qwen, FLUX.2 and Z-Image have been on disk
the whole time, unused for film work.

`engine: anime | qwen` is now a movie-level variable.

This is not a flag, because the two families want OPPOSITE prompt formats and feeding one
the other's is how you get abstract colour shapes. A beat therefore carries two prompts:

  tags    danbooru, comma separated      -> the anime SDXL path
  prompt  prose                          -> the Qwen path

They used to be the same string, which was harmless only while the Qwen branch was
unreachable. Building the prose taught the same lesson three times over:

  - A character's `desc` is NARRATIVE ("Has never beaten his rival") and tells an image
    model nothing it can draw. Characters gain `prose`, a visual description, and it
    falls back to the danbooru tags rather than to desc.
  - The emotion was missing from the prose entirely - the physical face tags that make
    `emotion` work at all were only being assembled for the anime path.
  - `prose` carries ONLY what never changes: face, hair, build. The garment stays in
    wear_tags, exactly as on the anime path, or the jersey gets described twice - once
    pristine and once damaged - and the earlier one wins.

The film's house style is appended last and skipped when it contradicts the engine.
Asking for "cel shading" on a photoreal render is asking for two pictures at once.

Compiling with engine:qwen warns that faces are held by reference sheets through
Qwen-Edit rather than by IPAdapter, which is a weaker lock. Verified rendering: 12-17s
per keyframe against Animagine's 4.5s.

KNOWN GAP: the reference sheets on disk are anime-styled, so a genuinely photoreal film
needs new ones. The engine switch is real; matching character sheets are not there yet.

Also: Illustrious-XL-v2.0 finished downloading (6.94 GB) and is registered as a
checkpoint, still status "untested".

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Make the checkpoint a comparable variable, and fetch a second anime model
entries.body:
An inventory turned up the largest gap in the project: animagine-xl-4.0 is the ONLY
anime checkpoint on the box, and there are ZERO SDXL anime LoRAs. Every LoRA present is
for Qwen, FLUX, LTX or Wan. So the entire anime image path - every film, every one of the
1026 capability panels - has run on one base model with no style range at all. That is
the likeliest explanation for the early complaint that output was "cartoony but not
anime-like": there was nothing else to be.

Current practice treats Animagine 4.0 as the starter model and Illustrious-family
checkpoints as the daily driver, so Illustrious-XL-v2.0 is downloading (6.94 GB). Its
earlier download on 2026-07-31 failed and was never retried.

studio/checkpoints/ is a new library, and `checkpoint` is now a varyable in the gallery.
It is the only variable that changes the SAMPLER SETTINGS as well as the prompt, so each
card carries its own steps, cfg, sampler and quality tags - comparing two models at a
third model's settings measures nothing. Animagine: 28 steps, cfg 5.0, its four
load-bearing quality tokens. Illustrious: 28 steps, cfg 5.5, a shorter quality stack.

Illustrious ships as status "untested" and stays that way until it has been rendered
beside Animagine on identical prompts and seeds. A recommendation is not a measurement.

Node ids for the sampler were read out of 22_anime_kf_ipadapter.json rather than guessed
- an earlier draft of this patch sprayed steps/cfg at four candidate nodes and would have
silently set none of them.

Also: a dry run no longer reports its skipped work as "failed".

entries.subject: Drop the saturation flag - it was measuring intent and calling it failure
entries.body:
The gallery flagged 79 of its first 220 generations. 76 of those were near_greyscale,
and every one was a false positive.

The values it fired on hardest were bleach, bleach_bypass and noir, at 100% each -
looks whose entire job is to remove colour. Flagging them is flagging a black-and-white

entries.subject: Render from the wizard, so nobody has to open a terminal
entries.body:
The Review tab previously wrote a .movie file and printed two commands to go and run
somewhere else. For anyone who is not already comfortable in a shell that is where the
tool stopped being usable - you could author a scene but not see it.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Make per-shot camera real, and remove an injury from an expression
entries.body:
A validation pass over the 90 newly authored presets found three blocking defects.
Two were real and are fixed here. The third was not, and the reason is instructive.

1. PER-SHOT CAMERA WAS INERT - and the hole was in code added yesterday.
   All 20 templates set a camera on each shot. wizard.html stored it on the beat and
   movieText() never emitted it; the .movie grammar had no beat-level camera; so
   compile.py stamped every beat with the SCENE camera. noir_interrogation asks for
   push / static / push / static and compiled to four statics, losing the only
   movement the scene was built around. dawn_hope rendered four identical tilts.
   Three template notes asserted the opposite in so many words.

   short.py has always honoured beat["camera"] - it strips the template's move fx and
   substitutes this one. Nothing could express it, so the grammar gains
   `shot: TEMPLATE @camera | desc`. A roadmap camera warns and falls back to the
   scene's rather than silently rendering static.

   Verified: a scene with camera:static now compiles to static / push / static / pull
   exactly as authored, and @dolly_zoom warns.

2. emotions/defiance carried "blood on face" in its `face` field. An injury is not an
   expression, and sitting before the wear tags it outranked them - defiance at wear:0
   rendered a wounded face above an explicitly clean uniform. Damage belongs to the
   wear ladder, which exists to own it and to never decrease. Stale gallery records
   dropped so the running loop regenerates them.

3. NOT FIXED, because it was not a defect: looks/firelight and looks/neon were reported
   as darkening by 1.2% and 3.6%, far below this project's own 5.3% "i.e. nothing"
   threshold. That measurement was taken against testsrc2 - a bright synthetic pattern.
   Measured against a real ungraded night keyframe they darken by 15.3% and 33.2%.
   The check made exactly the error it was warning about: a synthetic pattern proves a
   filter chain PARSES, never what it does to actual content.

entries.subject: Encyclopedia, scene templates, and a gallery where every image carries its recipe
entries.body:
LIBRARY, widened. Authored in parallel and validated before installing: every one of
the 18 new grade strings was executed as real ffmpeg, ids were checked against the
live library, and all 20 templates were checked to reference only implemented values.

  looks      7 -> 25    the highest-value category, because a grade is EXACT
  emotions   9 -> 27    physical face tags, never the feeling word
  cues       8 -> 22
  weather    9 -> 19
  lighting   8 -> 18
  templates  0 -> 20

Deliberately NOT widened, because it would be adding fake choices: `shots` and
`cameras` are bound to scene_templates.py and fx_chain(), so new values need code,
not JSON. `transitions` are ignored by short.py entirely.

GALLERY. studio/_tools/gallery_gen.py grows a corpus by holding a template still and
varying exactly ONE variable across its values. Every generation appends a record with
the template, the variable being demonstrated, the complete resolved variable set, the
literal prompt and negative, seed, model, workflow, sampler settings and grade - so any
image can be reproduced, altered by one knob, and compared.

It is idempotent and resumable (deterministic ids, skip what exists) and --loop keeps it
cycling, so an idle GPU has something useful to do.

SELF-AUDITING. Each generation measures its own luma and saturation and flags itself
outside a readable range. This immediately caught something: the new look grades were
validated against testsrc2, a bright synthetic pattern, which proves a chain PARSES but
not that it produces a usable picture. Applied to a night scene, bleach and
bleach_bypass crush the subject to a near-black silhouette - luma 25 and saturation
under 1.3 - while remaining perfectly valid ffmpeg. Those records now carry too_dark and
near_greyscale rather than sitting in the library looking fine.

studio/gallery.html + /api/gallery: browse by variable, value or template, search the
prompt text, hide flagged results, and open any image for its full recipe and the
command that reproduces it.

The manifest is tracked; the images are gitignored, being regenerable from it.

entries.subject: Scene templates: API, wizard Start step, and a showcase renderer
entries.body:
A template is a one-click bundle that sets every variable at once AND brings its
own shots, so you begin from something that works rather than a blank page. Each
is shown with a rendered example and its settings visible on the card - nothing

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Add scripts/studio.sh - one command to run the whole studio
entries.body:
start / stop / restart / status / logs for the web app and ComfyUI together. The
app is useless without ComfyUI, since every render it triggers goes through it, so
they are managed as one thing.

Two rules the script follows, both learned on this box:

  Processes are found by WHICH PORT THEY HOLD, never by pkill -f. A pattern like
  "main.py --listen" matches the bash -c wrapper of the ssh command running it and
  kills your own session.

  Nothing is reported as started until the port has been observed listening. The
  first version of the boot script logged success immediately after launching the
  server, which read as OK during the window when it was not yet bound.

boot-services.sh now delegates to it and only adds the boot-specific part (waiting
for the network), so there is one implementation rather than two that drift.

~/shared/studio_start.sh is a thin wrapper so it sits alongside samba_start.sh and
ssh_start.sh where the other launchers are kept.

Tested: stop, start from cold, status when down, and an idempotent second start.

entries.subject: Give a shot a description, wrap dialogue captions, stop hot compounding
entries.body:
Three defects found by watching the first film the studio layer produced, rather
than by reading its logs.

1. A SHOT COULD NOT SAY WHAT WAS HAPPENING.
   `shot: sakuga` carried only a template name. A beat's entire prompt was
   identity + emotion + wear + look + place, and an anime checkpoint handed
   nothing but a character description renders the only thing it can: that
   character, posed, standing still. Every shot came back a portrait - including
   the sakuga beat that is supposed to be the money shot of the episode.

   The line is now `shot: TEMPLATE | what is happening`, spliced in exactly where
   screenplay.py has always put it: after identity and garment-state, before the
   world, because earlier and more specific tags win. A shot with no description
   gets a framing hint instead of nothing.

2. DIALOGUE CAPTIONS NEVER WRAPPED.
   wrap_caption existed and was only ever called on story captions. drawtext does
   not wrap, so a spoken line ran off both sides: "Nine years. Nine years we have
   come here and gone home quiet." rendered as "ne years. ... gone home qui",
   losing the start AND the end while still looking deliberate. They are set at
   cw*0.036 against story captions' cw*0.026, so they wrap tighter (34), and
   stack upward so a two-line caption grows away from the frame edge.

3. `hot` COMPOUNDED INTO MAGENTA.
   fx_chain appends `hot` last, so it lands on whatever came before. Stacked on
   `glow` - which screen-blends a blurred bright copy - its saturation 1.18 plus
   vibrance 0.22 blew the climax into an unreadable purple smear. The sakuga
   template asks for exactly that pair on its final cut. `hot` now keeps its
   contrast and gives up its saturation when any brightening effect is already in
   the chain. Verified surgical: a shot with neither is byte-identical.

entries.subject: Point every script at 127.0.0.1 instead of a hardcoded LAN IP
entries.body:
DHCP moved the box from .46 to .45 and nine scripts broke at once, each with its
own hardcoded os.environ.setdefault("COMFY_HOST", "192.168.1.46:8188").

These scripts run ON the box, so there was never a reason to route their render
requests over the network. That matters more than the address change: the NIC is
currently measured dropping 10% of ICMP and failing a 5 MB transfer outright
(RTL8126 on the in-kernel r8169 driver), so anything crossing it is unreliable.
Loopback avoids the fault entirely and cannot be moved by DHCP.

COMFY_HOST still overrides for driving a remote instance.

entries.subject: Audio/picture offset (L-cuts), and a voice-overlap guard that found a real bug
entries.body:
audio_lead on any beat, in seconds, negative to bring a line in early. transition:
l_cut / j_cut is sugar for -0.6s on the scene's FIRST spoken line, which is the only
place the overlap means anything. Off by default.

Reading the code changed the design. The roadmap assumed audio was welded to its shot;
it is not. cut() mixes each voice with adelay at its start and plays the WHOLE file, so
audio already runs past the end of its own shot - the `length` value only drives caption
display. The one thing that needed to move was the START.

Also: studio/transitions/l_cut.json and j_cut.json define these the OPPOSITE way round
from standard film usage (standard: L-cut is outgoing audio lagging, J-cut is incoming
audio leading). Both presets are now marked ready and carry the discrepancy in their
description rather than being silently renamed.

THE GUARD FOUND SOMETHING BIGGER. It warns when two voice cues collide, and fired on the
first run: VIRO runs 1.59s into MANAGER. That is not caused by the offset - VIRO's line
is 4.20s against a shorter beat, so it already spilled ~0.99s and nothing had ever
reported it.

Root cause is structural. FILMCRAFT.md's first law says to speak every line first,
measure it, then derive shot length from the real duration. epic.py does this. short.py
does NOT - it renders clips before voices and sizes every shot from a fixed template, so
any line longer than its template silently overruns. Diagnosed and documented in
HANDOVER.md; fixing it means reordering the stage graph, which is not an hour's work.

The example scene is reverted to a plain cut, because this film's timing cannot absorb a
lead until shot length follows speech length.

entries.subject: Wire emotion presets into prompts as physical tags
entries.body:
studio/emotions/ held nine presets built from physical descriptors - grief is
"crying, grieving / tears, downcast eyes / trembling / hunched" - and their own note
claimed they "render today as tags". Nothing read them. compile.py had no emotion
variable at all.

wear 0, because above that the damage state already owns posture and two posture claims
fight each other.

Order is load-bearing. identity -> face -> garment-in-its-damaged-state -> world. Earlier
and more specific wins when tags conflict, which is the same mechanism that made wear
fail when the damage trailed a pristine garment description.

line "...Again." now renders downcast eyes, tears on the cheeks and a downturned mouth. A
second scene set emotion: determined renders sharp eyes and a furrowed brow. Both match
their preset unmistakably.

nouns, not adjectives - the same finding that drove the look grade fix and the wear fix.

letting the audio half of an emotion preset silently do nothing.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Capability cards: measure whether the panels isolate the variable, and fix the ones that cannot
entries.body:
panel_diff.py measures every card two ways: difference at 160x90 (the variable plus
any recomposition) and at 16x9 (gross layout only). Result over 134 cards: 133 differ
in gross COMPOSITION between their options.

For shot.size that is correct - extreme_wide and extreme_close should be different
pictures. For grade.grain_size it is fatal: its four panels are four unrelated
portraits at different framings with no visible grain difference at all. The card
claims to show what grain looks like and shows nothing of the sort. Every panel uses
one subject sentence and one seed, but changing any token shifts SDXL conditioning
enough to recompose the shot.

So a prompt-driven panel can only demonstrate a variable whose effect IS composition.
For anything applied after generation, take ONE base image and apply the real filter.

deterministic_panels.py does that, using the actual implementation from short.py
rather than a copy of it:

  shot_fx_deterministic   8 panels - none/glow/flash/aberr/shake/smear/hot/whiteout
  look_deterministic      7 panels - every look preset's grade

Both are exact, reproducible, and show precisely what the renderer will do. The look
card in particular is now readable at a glance: identical stadium in all seven panels,
only the grade differs.

This is the same correction the camera sweep needed - hold everything still except
the one variable, or you are measuring the wrong thing.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Wire the authoring layer to the renderer, and make look actually work
entries.body:
compile.py now emits everything short.py reads. It previously produced a film dict
with no sheets, no anime_sheets, no voices and no music, so any .movie file with a
spoken line died on KeyError cfg["voice"] partway through a render. That gap had
been reported four times and never closed, which meant the entire studio layer -
461 variables, 98 presets, 206 cards, the web app - could not produce one frame.

  studio/characters/  3 character cards (tags, reference sheet, voice)
  studio/cues/        8 reusable score cues
  compile.py          emits anime_sheets / sheets / characters / voices / music,
                      splices character tags and WEAR into beat prompts, sets
                      beat.ref, and places score cues on the MEASURED timeline via
                      beat_seconds() instead of hand-written offsets
  compile.py          enforces the movie-level locks it has always documented
  compile.py          refuses at compile time when a speaker has no card, instead
                      of letting short.py discover it mid-render

Proven: studio/movies/derby-ep1.movie renders end to end. 12 beats, 17 shots,
40.3s, 1920x1080, audio duration matching video, -10.43 LUFS / -1.08 dBTP.

short.py - per-beat colour grade.
  Every look preset carries a distinct tuned grade string; compile.py wrote one
  onto every beat; make_cut never read it and applied a hardcoded night chain to
  everything. So night, cold, golden and day_for_night all produced the same
  picture and look appeared to do nothing. After the fix the look:cold window went
  from mean luma 81.5 to 115.5, while look:night stayed at 50.0 because its grade
  IS the old night chain - a control showing the change is surgical.

short.py - archive instead of overwrite. The output directory comes from the title
  alone, so two films sharing a title silently clobbered each other. A 334 MB,
  8m46s delivered episode was one ffmpeg -y away from being replaced by a test.

short.py - default COMFY_ROOT to ~/ComfyUI, matching epic.py.

serve.py - threaded, binds all interfaces, correct MIME types, /wizard route.

studio/wizard.html - a step-by-step director in render-dependency order: format
  locks, look and pace, place and time, cast, shots, review. Every choice is
  labelled with WHERE it takes effect - deterministic post, graph parameter,
  prompt tag, or not implemented - because two knobs that look identical in a form
  can be an exact ffmpeg operation and a suggestion to a diffusion model.

studio/effects.json - that tier map as data, citing the code that consumes each.

Card panels re-encoded PNG to WebP: 458 MB to 30.9 MB, 14.8x smaller. Contact
sheets: one image per card instead of eight, which is what makes verifying the
1026 never-looked-at panels tractable. 134 sheets, 5.3 MB.

Camera sweep, measured for the first time rather than inferred: all eight moves
land and the directions are correct mirrors. The first attempt swept a generated
clip and produced eight identical-looking panels, because that clip content
changed by 78.6 between first and last frame and swamped a 100px camera shift.
Swept against a still instead.

entries.author: sechang11
entries.subject: Initial commit: comfy-studio
entries.body:
An AI film studio on one RTX 5090. Three layers:

  scripts/   the renderers. short.py (generate few clips, cut them into many
             shots, add energy in post) and epic.py (long-form narrated).
  studio/    the authoring layer. A MOVIE > CHAPTER > SCENE text format, a
             461-variable census, 98 presets in 12 categories, 206 capability
             cards showing what each option value actually looks like, and a
             local web app to browse it all.
  craft/     what has been measured about filmmaking on this box - cutting
             rates, loudness targets, which camera moves survive, which
             prompt orderings work for which model family.

State of the work is in STATE.md, reconstructed and adversarially verified.
